GREENSBORO, N. C., June 24.—The lynching of the two men a few days since in Stokes County for rape, and the lynching of another one two weeks ago, does not seem to have had the effect looked for by the lynchers. This morning as Lizzie Fluch, a little 10-year-old daughter of Mrs. Jennie Fluch, living near Hillsboro, was on her way to the spring, she was accosted by William Gauch, a negro of bad character. The second made an infamous proposal to the girl, who, frightened by the look in his eyes, attempted to run away. He caught her and committed a rape upon her person. He at once died, and the child now lies in a precarious condition. Citizens of the county are looking for him.

Intelligence has reached here also of an infamous offense of a similar nature at Martinsville yesterday evening. Charles Gilmor, a negro, actually went into the house of Mr. Prince Winchester, white he and his wife were absent. The sole occupant of the house at the time was Miss Winchester. Knowing Gilmor, she asked him what he wanted, and suspecting that he had crept into the house for the purpose of robbery, she ordered him out. The negro, glaring boldly at her, told her he had no idea of leaving yet, and then went on to tell her to keep quiet on pain of death. At once guessing his horrible design, the young woman began to scream for help. Gilmor attempted to commit his devilish design upon her person, and despite her great struggles would have accomplished his purpose had he not been frightened off by the sound of footsteps of neighbors attracted by the girl's screams. He barely had time to leap from the rear window before they entered the house. Posses of citizens have been hunting him all day. This is the third offense of this character committed by Gilmor. Once he was convicted of an attempt at rape and sentenced to nine years in the Penitentiary, but his counsel succeeded in having his sentence shortened. He was a few years after convicted of rape and sentenced to twenty years in the Penitentiary, but after serving nine years he was released.

IN MEMORIAM.
Death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer—Meeting of the Official Board of Tryon Street Church, Charlotte.

The recent death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer, late of Edenton Street Church, Raleigh, former pastor of Tryon Street Charlotte, has affected the hearts of his former charge with deepest sorrow, and is felt in the whole community. During his pastoral charge of Tryon Street Church, through a period of four years, his ministry was marked by gentleness, faithfulness and ability—the most perfect esteem, affection, and confidence of his flock was maintained, while not a single discord occurred to mar the harmony of the relation between pastor and people.

The impress that he left upon this community was only for good. The fervency of his piety, the purity of, and transparency of his character, the simplicity and geniality of his social life, and the attractiveness of his preaching made him a general favorite in his own Church and won the admiration and esteem of the community.

Richly endowed with these qualities, he was prepared to be a "workman that need not be ashamed"—a faithful shepherd to those "over whom the Holy Ghost made him overseer"—a "wise master-builder" in the temple of the Lord—attractive and loving in the social circle, patient toward the erring, kind and tender in the sick room and house of mourning.

Deeply impressed with his character, we are deeply affected by his early death. We feel that we and the whole Church have suffered a great loss. We feel that the grief of his family is our grief, and the grief of the Church.

Hence, as we are bowed with a common sorrow, we mingle our tears with theirs. While wife, and father, and mother, and child, sit solitary in the shadow of this great grief, our hearts not only feel a kindred pang, but respond in sympathy and condolence to the appeal that comes from bleeding hearts.

Again we are impressed with the inscrutable mystery of Providence in removing a life so full of promise to the Church, just as it was approximating its prime, while there are so many waste places uncultivated and harvests ungathered. The workmen fall, still work goes on. The soldier dies at his post, still the battle does not cease; nor are the banners furled. "God buries His workmen, but carries on His work." So is it ever. We reverence this wisdom. We bow to this power. We adore this goodness. We are subdued under a sense of infinity!

While we stand with uncovered head in the presence of the Disposer of events, and bow our hearts in profoundest grief, we recognize in it the special providence of God, who is "too wise to err and too good to be unkind." Thus endeavoring to submit to the supreme decision of the Head of the Church, and to acquiesce in all the developments of His providence, we, the officers of Tryon Street Church, representing in this case the sentiments of the whole Church, while expressing our own sorrow at the death of our former pastor and friend, desire most heartily and sincerely to express to the bereaved family of the deceased our deepest sympathy; and we do most devoutly pray that God, in whose service he lived, labored, and died, may communicate to them His richest consolations in this trying hour, and so sanctify this afflictive dispensation of His providence as that it shall prove to them a blessing, both for time and eternity.

It was ordered that this communication be sent to the Charlotte papers and Raleigh Christian Advocate for publication—also that a copy be sent to Mrs. A. A. Boshamer as a testimony of our sympathy and affectionate regard.

OFFICIAL BOARD.
Charlotte, N. C., Oct. 13, 1881.

Local Items.

There have been fine rains in this section this week, greatly encouraging farmers in their small-grain work. While there have been killing frosts in the central part of the State two weeks ago, vegetation about here has scarcely been nipped or colored by frost.

A workman, W. A. Sing, in Mr. Josiah Asbury's planing mill, had his hand nearly severed from the wrist by a buzz saw. The saw caught his wrist band which drew the arm also. He will be detained from work some time.

The Almanac sellers or drummers on the streets are about as big a nuisance as the boot-blacks in New York.

Considering the very dry and hot Summer and Fall, the health of Charlotte has been remarkably good, equal to any Mountain city or town.

Sheriff Mays, of Alexander county, considering it unsafe to keep the murderer of Miss Thompson, E. H. Dockery, in the Alexander jail, or even in the jail of any adjoining county, brought the prisoner to this city to be committed to jail here. It was through Dockery's confession that Church, one of the murderers, was lynched, and it is thought his testimony in Court will seriously implicate two others. One, Adams, is under bond to appear at Court now. Evidently it was the friends of these that lynched Church.

The notorious female Minstrels are advertised to appear in Wilmington at an early day. There is an Ordinance in this city against permitting such vulgar performances in the Opera House or elsewhere in Charlotte.

The Hornet's Nest Riflemen of this city, about 30 in number, went to the Yorktown Centennial celebration, under command of E. F. Young.

A Woman Charged with Barn-Burning Lynched.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

CHARLESTON, S. C., April 14 — The barn of J. S. Blalock, at Martin's Depot, in Laurens county, was burnt on the 3d instant. The barn was near the dwelling, and it is supposed that the latter was intended to be burnt. On Saturday the 9th Judy Metts (colored), living at Blalock's, was arrested as the incendiary by a constable, who started with her for Clinton about 8 P. M. He had gone two miles when he was overtaken by a number of masked men on horseback. Some took the constable in charge; others the woman. The constable was kept one hour, then told to "git." The woman was found next morning hanged to a tree 200 yards from where she was taken by the lynchers.

The coroner's jury on Monday found a verdict "hanged by persons unknown." No efforts have been made to discover the lynchers. The same woman was accused of burning a dwelling two years ago, but was not tried.

Once they handled no one but murderers whom they feared might have personal influence enough to escape conviction; then a poor year for murderers having deprived them of their customary sport they strung up scoundrels who had assaulted women, and who consequently would have been safe of conviction. Lynch Law.
Lynch Law.

There is no State in the Union, in which this old time method of met ing out justice to criminals is not resorted to in cases of heinous crimes committed with premeditation and under circumstances of great aggravation. With the progress of law and civilization it is rarely exercised though common in wild and newly settled regions. In a country like ours it is never excusable, though cases arise, at times, which seem to call for swifter punishment than is obtainable under the slow process of law. In no case do we believe that calm reflection will approve lynch law, not only because it is a violation of law, but because innocent life may be taken under the excitement created by an atrocious crime. We have judges, jurors and all officials necessary to the punishment of crime, and the enforcement of law according to law has a wholesome influence on society, while the violation of law has a demoralizing tendency. A case of lynching a negro woman occurred in Laurens County, two miles above Clinton on the 9th instant. The barn of Mr. Blalock had been set on fire and burned on the 3d instant and the barn was so near the dwelling house that it was considered an attempt to burn it also. Suspicion pointed to Judy Metts, a negro woman living on his place, and who had been charged two years ago with burning the dwelling of Mr. Simpson. On the 9th a warrant was sworn out against her and on Saturday night she was arrested by a constable, who started with her for Clinton. About two miles from Martin's Depot a party of disguised men took both the constable and prisoner in charge, and while some retained the constable others took off the prisoner. On Sunday morning her body was found hanging to a tree about 200 yards from the point the lynchers took her in charge. At the inquest on Monday the coroner's jury returned a verdict that she came to her death by hanging, at the hands of parties unknown. No one has been arrested and so far none of the party is known. While arson is a high crime, punishable with death, unless the jury recommend the party to mercy, still it is not of a character to call for lynching, especially when the building was not a dwelling house. To permit such highhanded violations of law in such cases tends to disorganize society and government and to lead people to become judges and executioners in all cases. When the crime is horrible as in rape and murder combined &c., then much allowance can be made for over excitement and ultra legal remedies, but in this case no such excuse exists.

cowan-martins-depot-1881-04-09.A27:
A Woman Hanged by a Mob in Laurens County.
The habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes in this State has gone on constantly for several years, and without censure, but now we are glad to see that two or three journals of the State have had the manhood to denounce the recent hanging of the half-witted negro woman in Laurens county.—Abbeville Press and Banner.

The hanging of this woman by a mob can not be too severely condemned, and we trust the officers of the law in Laurens County will ferret out the guilty parties and have them punished according to the enormity of their crime. The zeal of our esteemed contemporary in this direction is to be commended, but when it accuses the people of the State of "the habit of lynching weak and defeseless negroes," we think it is going farther than the facts will justify. The only lynching in the State that we remember, up to the time of the lynching of this woman, was for the heinous offense of rape and murder. The first fiend who met the vengeance of an outraged community for rape, was John J. Moore, a white man in Spartanburg county. Then followed the lynching of three negroes in Clarendon county for the brutal murder of a white woman and plundering of the house, and the lynching of the two negro brutes at Prosperity for the outrage and murder of Miss Wertz.

The indiscrtminate charge of murder and lawlessness against our people is common with the Radical sheets of the North, but the Press and Banner is the first Democratic paper in the State, or the South, which has made a similar charge. It would have been better for the good reputation of our contemporary to have given the number of "weak and defenseless negroes" lynched, and the character of the offenses for which they were lynched. If it had persued this course and then given its unqualified condemnation of the persons who committed the deeds and the papers who commended them, there would have been some consistency in its course, but when it makes a wholesale charge against the people of the State without giving the number of "weak and defenseless" negroes lynched, and the character of their offenses, we think it is placing itself in a very unenviable position to say the least of it. No doubt its assertion will be copied by all the bloody shirt organs of the North, and quoted upon every political rostrom by Republican speakers, as the highest Democratic evidence that their charges against the white people of the South are true. Such reckless and unjust charges are calculated to do us more harm than the treachery of all the Mahonns in the South.

The trial of men for their lives always develops in the public mind a feeling of interest, and, no matter how guilty the accused may be, there is, in the hearts of those far away from the aggravating scenes, a feeling of sympathy for those who may be sentenced to death, and the mind naturally runs over any facts which may excite a doubt as to the guilt of the accused, or which may exhibit any unusual zeal on the part of the all-powerful Government in its efforts, under the forms of law, to put one of its citizens to death. The money of the Government to employ detectives we presume was not spared in this particular case, and the detectives for their energy and fidelity to the work which they had undertaken deserve commendation. The Governor also has shown a commendable interest in the matter, and in order to make competent the testimony of Fletcher Maddux, that officer showed his interest in the matter when he pardoned him out of the penitentiary and removed his disabilities, incurred by other felonies for the express purpose of convicting his comrades or associates in crime. And then as the crowning act in this drama, which is to end in a tragedy, besides an able and efficient Soliciter, Mr. M. F. Ansel, one of the best lawyers in Greenville, and Col. W. E. Earle, formerly of Greenville, but now of Washington, D. C., were employed to assist the State in the prosecution. Everybody knows that no man in upper South Carolina wields a greater influence before a jury than Colonel Earle. With an array of counsel like this, when it is remembered that one criminal was pardoned out of the penitentiary to get sufficient evidence to convict, and the zeal of the detectives is fresh in our minds, it is easily to be seen that the State has done its whole duty in its efforts to convict these men, and if it were customary for the State so to act, it would not now be a matter of note. As evidence of the extraordinary zeal manifested to convict these men, we may be pardoned for referring to the murder of Judy Metts, in Laurens where, it is supposed five, or six, or possibly eight, white men hanged this negro in the night time. If any effort, except the offering of a reward by the Governor, has been made to arrest the perpetrators of this crime, we have not heard of it. In this we would not blame our most excellent Governor, because we know that he cannot do much to correct evil, except where he has the aid and sympathy of the community in which crime has been committed. We presume that nobody in Laurens county wants to see respectable white men hanged for the murder of a Judy Metts, who was a half-crazy negro, and, as a matter of course, friendless. The Greenville incendiaries committed their offence against the sentiment of a powerful community, who will be able to have the offenders punished.

We put fault at no man's door in this matter, nor do we blame the Government at all. The fact is, we merely remark upon a state of society which punishes one class of criminals to the full extent of the law, while another class need not fear being brought into court.

Now, for the condemned men at Greenville: In the first place they had no money to employ counsel, and had to accept such services as lawyers were willing to render without pay. Solicitor Orr in open court, when speaking of their lawyers, pronounced the leading counsel which they had, as not "responsible for what he said, but regarded him as a crazy man."

We suppose that three stronger men could not have appeared for the State than Orr, Ansel, and Earle. Taking the State Solicitor's remarks about the defendants council as true, the contest seems to have been an unequal one, and, no matter how guilty, we confess our sympathy for men convicted and sentenced to death under circumstances like these.

Repenting at Leisure.

NEW YORK, December 3d.—The evening papers have the following: About two years ago the daughter of Amos Stillman, of Brooklyn, eloped with W. S. Guild. Miss Stillman was only about 16, while Guild was 70. After a private marriage ceremony, they slipped away to Europa without the knowledge of relations or friends. Things were not just what the young bride thought they would be, and in four days she became home-sick and prevailed upon Guild to return. When they reached the wharf in New York he hired a coach and sent her home to her parents, while he got upon another steamer and set sail for California. Fools and Damphools.
The world has agreed for the sake of convenience to divide its fools into two species. One it calls simply a fool; the other, to adopt the word which Doesticks applied to his friend, it calls a damphool. This is used strictly in its scientific, not its profane, and has nothing in common with the shallow and random use which angry men make of it to give vent to their momentary irritation. A fool is often harmless, and may be snubbed and kept in order. A damphool cannot be. A fool is often tolerable and docile. If he cannot be taught much wisdom, he can be taught obedience and respect. But though a damphool may have intelligence, he has little or no reverence. A fool may have some humor, but a damphool has none. A tool can be made a fool of; a damphool makes a fool of himself. A fool may have a little sense, but whatever other sense a damphool may possess, he is sure to lack common sense. A fool may be humble and retiring, but it is the essence of his kinsmen to be conceited and self-asserting. A fool generally knows he is a fool, and so is often doleful when he thinks of it; but a damphool never knows it, and so is happy. A fool is often stupid, headless, blundering, aimless, like a hen or a fly; the other is strutting, irritating, conceited, like a turkey and a peacock; or a noisy nuisance, like a June beetle. A fool is often patient, well-digposed, and, though slow, good-natured, like the ass; but his foster brother is apt to bear malice, and is intelligently obstinate like the mule.

To the ranks of the odious kind of fool belong those who hanker morbidly for notoriety—the Tanners, the Bradlaughs, the Guiteaus, the Booths, the Count Johannes and George Francis Trains. Poor Train, however, has stepped down and out of the ranks, and now appears to be simply and only a fool. The fool is an object of sympathy, of pity, compassion and help; his robust relative gives cause for disgust, for sport, for derision and ridicule. Shakspeare, of course, saw the difference between these types, and has drawn them with his usual clearness and acuteness. His fools and clowns are famous—Touchstone and Dogberry; Launce, Slender old Gobbo, and the like; but his damphools—such as Justice Shallow, Pistol, Falstaff, Polonious, old Capulet, have equal rights to consideration. When, in the play of “Midsummer Night’s Dream,” the dramatist changed Bottom the Weaver into an ass, he turned his damphool into a simple fool. For Bottom the Weaver imagines he can write a play, take the chief role and be stage manager all at the same time, making himself poussed and ridiculous, indeed; but changed into an ass he is docile and humble and wants only to have his head scratched and to be fed on dried peas and good sweet hay.

A fool may be pious and reverential, believe in creeds and religion; but the other sort is quite likely to be an atheist. David undoubtedly meant to write that the damphool “hath said there is no God.”

A bloody double tragedy occurred at the town of Burton, Mo., on the Wabash railroad, on Wednesday. A man named Jackson insulted a lady named Langford. The lady told her husband, who at once hunted up Jackson, and began chastising him. Jackson drew a knife and stabbed Langford several times, inflicting mortal wounds. Benjamin Bird (colored), convicted of the murder of Policeman Nelson (colored) June 25, 1880, during the mill riot at Jacksonville, Fla., was executed at 12 o'clock, Friday, in the jail yard. A short time previous to the execution he made a confession of the crime to the sheriff and others, but while on the gallows protested his innocence. When the trap was sprung and Bird fell, the noose had not been properly arranged, the end slipped out and he fell to the ground. He got up with the assistance of the sheriff, and again walked upon the trap, the rope being properly adjusted, and he was launched into eternity.

Mrs Gately was the victim, and her husband's story is that she complained of feeling unwell, about 7:30 o'clock, and that she went to bed. Next foren o1, about 5 o'clock, he called her, but got no answer. He went into her room and found that the whole left side of her was crushed in and marks of violence all over her body. The bed was stained with blood, and there was evidence of a violent struggle. The walls and ceiling was also stained with blood. Her husband has been arrested for the crime, and the clothes that he wore have the appearance of having been washed. His handkerchief also contained brook sand. eight years respectively, were playing in the street on Washington avenue near Nineteenth street yesterday evening about four o'clock, when one of them was attacked by a ferocious bore hog. The residence of John Miller, a respectable planter living in Randolph county, was visited the other night by ten or twelve men, who were heavily armed and wore muslin masks on their faces. They surrounded the dwelling and called loudly for Miller to come out. Miller was absent, in attendance at a Baptist association some miles away, upon learning which, the mob entered the house, and taking two boys, aged fifteen and eighteen years, into the yard, whipped them in a terrible manner. The youngest boy in attempting to escape was fired on, no less than twenty shots taking effect in his body. He fell to the ground, and the desperadoes, after threatening the lives of Miller's wife and daughter, rode away, remarking that at the next visit they would clean out the whole ranche and kill every one about it. After they left Mrs. Miller followed them some distance without their knowledge, and identified some of them. No cause for the outrage is assigned. It was feared that Miller would be assassinated while returning homeward, but he is reported to have reached his family without molestation.

MISS ISHMAEL AVENGED.
A Mysterious Mob Appears at Midnight and Hangs Her Supposed Murderers on a Tree.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., March 11.—The soquel to the tragic murder of Miss Ishmael, near Jonesboro, Craighhead County, was learned to-day. The nogroes arrested on suspicion of the murder were Green Harris, John Woods, Olles Beck, and Burt Harkins. The were examined at New Haven Church, seven miles north of Jonesboro, before Justices of the Peace Akors and Jackson, and by them committed and ordered to jail to await the action of the Grand Jury at the approaching Circuit Court. Pending their removal to prison the prisoners were placed in the church under a strong guard, the intention being to lodge them in the Jonesboro Jail early the next morning. The examination drew together hundreds of people, and the excited crowd swarmed into the church during the examination of the accused or gathered on the grounds without the cellar discussing the tragedy in low, significant tones. The examination occupied some time, and night had fallen over it was concluded, when the prisoners had been disposed of as before stated, and the people began to withdraw.

Threats had been made of lynching, but many influential planters discounted such proceeding, urging that the law, if allowed to take its course, would avenge the crime. It was supposed that their counsel had effect, and that the prisoners would be dispatched by legal means. The guards around the church were doubled however, in anticipation of mob violence. This anticipation was unhappily realized. About the hour of midnight, when the guards were beginning to feel drowsy, they were aroused by the sound of approaching footsteps, which came from the vicinity of the adjacent woods.

The next instant, as if by magic, a crowd of masked men, variously estimated at from 200 to 300, sprang out from the shadows of the trees and, surrounding the church, dominated the prisoners. The request not being complied with, the guards were overpowered in a twinkling, the doors and windows of the rude frame building smashed in, and the terrified negroes dragged out and hustled to the nearest tree. The prisoners begged piteously for their lives, but their captors were deaf to all entreaty, and in less than fifteen minutes after their capture the four negroes were dangling in the

air in the agonies of death, all having been suspended on one and the same tree.

Having completed their ghastly work the lynchers alitently dispersed, leaving the bodies of their victims still hanging, and presenting a horrid spectacle in the pale moonlight, as the night winds awayed them to and fro. It is said that all the negroes confessed their guilt before they were hanged. The excitement in the vicinity of the scene has subsided. The better class of planters depreciate the means employed for the punishment of the crime, though they hold that the murderers of Miss Ishmael deserved swift justice.

West Virginia and the Mother State.

If there is any one point upon which the people of this State are substantially of one mind it is as to the perpetual separate Stateship of West Virginia. For many years there has not been a single public man, or a journal of any creed or party, that has expressed any inclination for a reunion. Even the border-line feeling in favor of it that was manifested in Greenbrier County just after the close of the War seems to have died out. At least we hear nothing more of it. The sense of a long course of injustice toward the people of West Virginia on the part of the old State, when we were a part of it, is still alive in this State among the older people, outside of any question of politics, and the younger generation have no traditions that are not West Virginian in their character. We are all looking forward hopefully to the day when West Virginia will be developed by railroads and be made one of the most prosperous States of the Union. The more the public know of the resources of West Virginia the more they realize that she has

the elements of a great future as a State. We do not want, therefore, to be hampered by any adverse policy, such as that which kept us back under the old régime, when the public money represented in the debt of Virginia was spent almost exclusively for the development of the territory outside of our borders.

GARRISON'S GRIT.

A Little "Sand" and a Handy Revolver Saved Him a Lynching—His Explanation of the Trouble with the Grangers and His Account of the Fire in the Cheese Factory.

Young Garrison, the Winfield cheesemaker, whose arrest for alleged incendiarism and whose narrow escape from a lynching at the hands of his angry creditors were referred to in a dispatch in yesterday's Tribune, was brought before the Justice of the Peace at Wheaton yesterday, and obtained a continuance until tomorrow. Young Garrison's explanation is that it had been customary to collect money for his patrons and hold it over from time to time, and no trouble had ever come of it until now. The reason he had not paid dividends to the Winfield farmers was that some of his October collections were behind, and he desired to make as large a payment as possible. The claims ranged from $20 to $500, and aggregated several thousand dollars. He had promised his patrons to pay them on Thursday last, and had on hand for that purpose $7,000 in greenbacks. Not desiring to keep this large sum in one place, where burglaries could get it in case they should raid the establishment, he divided it into three parcels, and hid it in a room on the second floor of the factory on Wednesday night. He then, in company with Mr. Frank Burroughs, the young man who was working in the factory, retired. They slept in an adjoining room, on the second floor, in which were their clothes and the books of the concern. About midnight Burroughs was aroused by a peculiar noise, and going to a window he discovered that

THE BOILER-ROOM WAS WRAPPED IN FLAMES
and the factory itself was being rapidly consumed. He roused Garrison, and they immediately endeavored to get into the adjoining room and secure the money they had placed there earlier in the evening, but it was too late. The room was filled with flame and smoke, and the floor and roof soon fell in. They seized a trunk of Garrison's and got it out of the building, but failed to secure anything else. The next day young Garrison was arrested for arson at the instance of some of his patrons, but before he could be taken to Wheaton, the farmers who had waited so patiently for their money heard of the occurrence of the night before and flocked to the scene in a very angry mood. A large number of these people had collected, and as their losses occurred to them they became enraged beyond control. Some one suggested that they hang him, and a rope was speedily procured, and the crowd started for the station where young Garrison was. When questioned on this point he admitted it to be true, and being asked what saved his neck, he replied, "If it had not been for a little 'sand' and a revolver in my pocket I would have been strung up." It appears, however, that Judge Drummond, who lives near Winfield, came on the scene at this time, and doubtless his presence had much to do toward pacifying the enraged farmers.

CHICAGO, November 28, 1881.

Corruption in Chicago courts received a death blow to-day at the hands of Judge Tuley, of the criminal bench. He dismissed a whole panel of jurors. Why? Simply because he considered those composing it to be men unworthy to act impartially. He avowed his purpose not to accept as a juror a man not of the highest reputation for integrity. This is a move in the right direction, and Judge Tuley deserves the greatest praise for taking the initiative in this much needed reform; but it is to be hoped that the bench throughout the city, and the whole country, will be influenced to adopt the same salutary measures.

Rowell, the great English pedestrian, is in Chicago. He considers young Dobler, of Chicago, the second best walker in the world. They are matched to walk at no far distant day.

The Pennsylvania railroad has commenced a prosecuting war on the "scalpers." How very strange it is that none of the "scalpers" are ever prosecuted successfully. A friend at my elbow intimates that the several railroads may, periodically, when passenger travel is light and funds short, "unload" tickets to the scalpers. By this dodge persons who could not pay full fare would be induced to buy low priced tickets. Thus an impetus would be given to travel and expenses to rolling stock be paid, while the regular full fare traffic would not be injured. My friend may be right. If so, then this hurrah against the poor scalper is all buncombe.

The Jews of Chicago are organizing for the relief of their brethren who are being driven from Russia, and who are coming to Chicago. This is a praiseworthy move.

The fiend who murdered Mr. Hessler, a German farmer of North Evanson, near Chicago, last week, as mentioned in my last letter to the LEDGER, has been caught and has confessed the crime. His name is John Galus and his age twenty-two. He says he struck his victim with a hatchet because he called him vile names. When he found he had killed him he put on the dead man's clothes, took his money and left the house. He seems very indifferent to his situation, evidently justifying himself for committing the terrible deed on the grounds that the old man drove him into a high passion by applying to him villainous epithets that reflected upon his mother's honor and virtue.

THE PALESTINE REGULATORS.
Their Threats and Assassinations Brought to an End by their Arrest.

CHICAGO, March 12.—Thirty-one persons, including several women, have been arrested at Palestine, Ohio, a little town near the Indiana line, for sending threatening letters to Jacob Long, a saloon keeper. The culprits are supposed to belong to a gang of regulators, formed two or three years ago, who have terrorized the village by their threats, and in two cases by downright assassination. In 1879, an old man named Guyere received a note warning him to leave town on pain of death. A few nights thereafter a horseman rode up to his door and hailed him. Guyere stepped out on the porch, and as he appeared in the lamplight twenty bullets pierced his body. His murderers escaped, and not one of them has ever been brought to justice. Later a negro named Stephen Wade was served in like manner. An effort was then made to ferret out the leaders, but the detectives found the band of regulators so strong that they gave up the task. Since then other persons have been served with notices to quit the country, and several of them, remembering the fate of Guyere and Wade, have emigrated. Long, the saloon keeper, however, refuses to go, and the arrests just made show that there is a prospect that the reign of the mob may be brought to an end.

THE LYNCHING AT QUINCY, FLA.
Graphic Description of the Hanging of Lunn Whittaker.
A Quincy Herald extra, issued on Sunday morning, gives the following additional particulars of the lynching of Lunn Whittaker:

"Some time between the hours of two and three o'clock this morning the county jail was entered by a crowd of twenty or thirty armed men, clad in blouses and well masked, who overpowered the jail guard and took a negro prisoner, Lunn Whittaker, from the room where he was confined, and proceeded with him about a quarter of a mile from the jail—into the woods just east of town—and hung him by the neck till he was dead, from a convenient limb of a black oak tree. The news of the lynching spread like wild fire. It was received with incredulity by the citizens of this law-abiding community, but a visit to the spot confirmed the fact. The work of the Vigilantes had been thoroughly though inartistically performed.

"The victim was hoisted with an ordinary plow-line, and the noose was so unscientifically adjusted—the knot tightening before touching his neck—that his suffering must have been horrible. He was a large, powerful man; had on a light colored pair of pantaloons, a dark coat, and had on one boot—a stocking only being on the other foot. The sight was a horrible one, though a large number viewed the remains.

"The guard, consisting of three or four young men of unimpeachable grit, were most unceremoniously 'bounced.' In order to relieve the motony of the situation, they were singing a song. In midst of the ditty, and before they could wink—Prestol they were surrounded, and looking down the muzzles of cocked navy revolvers—an average of about four pistols to each guard. Resistance would have been mere insanity. They were forced to accompany the lynchers, and witnessed the choking. The men were in dead earnest, and 'meant business' from the word 'go.' Whittaker fought desperately, but his time had arrived. He is probably in a warmer region than Florida, at present, as it was pretty thoroughly known that he was the prime cause of Jas. McJunkin's assassination."

CINCINNATI, April 18 — A dispatch from Batavia, Ohio, reports a murder at the village of Rural, on the Ohio River, and in Cermont county, last evening, at a singing school taught by a young Kentuckian, named Carr. Alf Reed and Harvey Kiebs, both roughs, created a disturbance and were reprimanded by Carr. On the way home Reed met and whipped Carr. Afterward Reed came into the drug store where Carr was, and the latter struck Reed with a scale weight, killing him, and escaped.

A dispatch from Hopkinsville, Christian county, Ky., reports that Kiah Baker, an old colored man, was shot and killed by an unknown person, last Friday night. He said he met three men on horseback, one of whom shot him. Other say he was shot while robbing a hen rost.

GALVESTON, April 18 — While circusmen were loading cars at the railroad crossing, three men leaving town insisted on crossing that particular place. A fight ensued, in which Campbell, one of the showmen, was seriously shot twice through the body. Two other citizens were seriously cut.

BOSTON, April 18 — Wandell Phillips filed a protest to the Governor and Council against the execution of Stearns K. Abbott, convicted of the murder of Mrs. Crue, and sentenced to be hanged on Friday next. Phillips contends, even admitting Abbott killed Mrs. Crue, there is no evidence showing he did it with premeditation or malice aforethought. Phillips, in ending his protest, says, "I do not care to enlarge on the motive which I think impels the Executive to commit this crime, which, in my view, makes the act murder in the strictest sense of the law."

JACKSONVILLE, FLA., April 18 — A colored man charged with the assassination of a leading citizen of Gadesen county some time since, was taken from jail in Quincy on Sunday by disguised men and hanged.

Lynch Law in the South.

PROSPERITY, S. C., April 18 — The lynching of the old negro woman, Eliza Cowan, alias Judith Metts, in Laurens county, is denounced by all right thinking people. The offense of the old woman was barn-burning, a crime punishable upon conviction in this State with death. The victim of mob law in this instance was a helpless and defenceless old woman. The county in which it occurred is one of the wealthiest in the State. Its inhabitants claim and are recognized as the most refined and intelligent people in the State of South Carolina. The lynching is denounced on all sides. No active or systematic steps, however, have yet been taken to arrest and punish the perpetrators of the crime.

ASSASSINATION OF AN OHIO WOMAN.
GORE, O., Dec. 28.—At 6:30 o'clock this evening an unknown man opened the door of the house of Mrs. Manley Terrell, a widow living on the outskirts of this place, and shot her through the heart. Her two grown daughters were in the room at the time, but can give no description of the murderer, the deed being so quickly done and it being dark. Mrs. Terrell was the mother of William Terrell, the young man now serving a life term in the Ohio Penitentiary for the triple murder of the Weldon family near this place four years ago. There is no clew to the murderer. Vigilance committees have been organized and are scouring the country.
morgan-richards-gore-1881-12-29.A2:
Arrest of the Assassin of Mrs. Terrell.
A special from Gove, Ohio, says the authorities placed a guard about the house of Mrs. Terrell, who was assassinated last night, to prevent the obliteration of the tracks of the assassin. As soon as daylight came, they found the track and traced the assassin to the residence of Mr. Arnold, a farmer, and arrested Morgan Richards, one of Arnold's farm hands, as the criminal. He was armed with a revolver which had one empty chamber. He resisted arrest, but was overpowered, placed in a wagon and driven rapidly to Logan jail, barely escaping a lynching party who tried to head him off. No motive for the crime has been developed.

Gone, Dec. 29.—Morgan Richards brutally assassinated Mrs. Mary Terrell last night.

morgan-richards-gore-1881-12-29.A8:
Emulating Guiteau.
CINCINNATI, December 29.—A special to the Commercial, from Gore, Ohio, says: Morgan Richards has confessed to the murder of Mrs. Terrill, his mother's sister, and says it was done on account of an old grudge. The murdered woman's son, William, is undergoing a life sentence in the penitentiary for the murder of three persons four years ago. Mr. Terrill died of grief for his son's crime two years ago. It is thought Richards shot his aunt to prevent her revealing what she knew about the others implicated in her son's crime. Richards is a young man, and has taken unusual interest in the Guiteau trial, particularly in what Guiteau says. A few days ago he bought a revolver, remarking that it was the same kind that Guiteau used. From this it is supposed that he did the murder for the sake of notoriety. There is still talk of lynching him.

DENVER, Col., Dec. 18. — A special from Leadville to the Tribune says: The Independence mining camp, 20 miles west of here, has for a long time been overrun with desperate characters, who kept it in a perpetual state of turmoil. Often several of these would band together and virtually take possession of the camp, shooting men down in the streets, and making it necessary for the citizens to close their stores and suspend business for several hours. Shortly after dark last night Patton and Malloy, two desperadoes having the reputation of killing a number of men, became intoxicated and began firing revolvers promiscuously. General indignation ensued, and the people turned out en masse and pursued the desperadoes, who were finally brought to bay and literally riddled with bullets. They returned the fire of the mob, but without effect. A little later a vigilance committee was formed for the purpose of hanging some of the worst blacklegs, but all of that class left town immediately after the shooting of Patton and Malloy.

Our community was startled and shocked on Tuesday morning last by the rumor, which proved to be founded on fact, that two of the prisoners in the jail had been taken from their cells on the previous night and hanged near the Bayou DeSiard road about two and a half miles from the court-house. These unfortunate parties were Alec Wilson, charged with the murder of Reuben Leonard and Perry Munson, charged with the murder of Anderson Mitchell—these, and their victims were all negroes. Both murders had been cold blooded and premeditated In the first case the victim was shot down at night and the other had his neck broken by a blow from a heavy bludgeon, whilst he was quietly walking on the roadside in company with his wife. In both cases the testimony against the prisoners was circumstantial but quite strong and convincing—still they had neither been proved guilty—and were both held in jail, subject to the investigation and action of the Grand Jury. The idea that our parish or its officers will arrest parties charged with the commission of crime and then fail to protect them is horrifying and revolting in the extreme. That a party of men can come to our parish seat, get possession of the jail keys, and without resistance commit such a crime as has startled our community this week as equally shameful and disgraceful. We trust and believe that the proper officers will investigate this matter to the bottom and make an example of all parties in any manner responsible for this barbarously cruel act.

The trouble grew out of a debt of 15 cents which a man named Leo claimed was due him from a man by the name of Jennings. The latter stoutly denies that he owed Leo anything. The dispute resulted in a fight, during which Leo stabbed the negro a number of times, inflicting injuries from which he shortly died. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., June 6.—Deputy United States Marshal Bolton reached Atlanta today with a bullet lodged in his body near his heart, which he received last night about 11 o'clock, in Forsyth County, while he and one or two men were attempting to capture two wagons loaded with "mountain dew." As the officers rode up to the wagons they were fired upon by several moonshiners. Bolton and his men returned the fire, but owing to their being outnumbered were obliged to retreat. CHAMPAIGN, Ill., June 5.—The prisoners in the County Jail at Urbana, this county, came near escaping last night. The bark Ibis, from Pensacola, lay yesterday at the foot of Seventeenth street, North river. A Sun reporter boarded her and asked Captain Sawyer if he had really seen whales off Pimlico Sound on his way up the coast last Saturday.

"Whales?" said the genial Captain, "Any number of them. There must have been two miles of black backs and water-spouts."

Capt. Sawyer unrolled a time-worn chart on the table in his cabin and with his dividers followed down a number of pencil marks to latitude 40 degrees and longitude 74 degrees 15 minutes. This brought him to a point about eighty miles off Pimlico Sound, and further northeast of Cape Hatteras.

"It was on Saturday and Sunday, he continued, "when we encountered these sperm whales going south of southwest, as if to go around Hatteras. They were going very slowly, backs above the water, and were spouting all of the time. They were strolling along in groups, sunning themselves half an hour at a time, and then taking a header and coming up to spout."

"How many were there?"

"Well, first we met two schools of about 100 each, I should say. Occasionally they frolicked and flopped about heavily in a sort of dignified and elephantine sport. More followed, and the next morning (Sunday) we saw more. Altogether there were over 700 on the picnic. We passed within 500 feet of two big fellows, but they seemed preoccupied and didn't notice the ship. I don't think they knew we were there."

"Had you any means of capturing them?"

"No, and it did seem a pity to have so much valuable sperm oil indolently swimming away from us. There were some big whales there, too. I said to Limerick, one of my men here, 'Now there's a fellow that's worth $2000,' and he must have been, and there were bigger ones in the school. It would have been a harvest for a whaling ship. A million dollars in sperm whales is too good a haul to let go by, but we couldn't do anything. Occasionally I have seen a

sperm whale cruising along as far south as Savannah, and once in a while I've heard of whale ships off about there. But I never saw so many whales at one time before anywhere."

"Where were they going?"
"For squids, probably. That's a favorite food with them."

"Is there any danger to be feared from them?"
"No; they're harmless. I think I never heard of more than one case where a whale attacked a vessel, and that's in ancient history. Over a hundred years ago, I believe, the ship Easex was run down by a mad whale. My own experience with whales has been that they are shy, and if they upset a boat, do it by accident in trying to get away."

OKOLONA, MISS.

A Negro Murderer Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color.

OKOLONA, July 30.—About three weeks ago Robert Barker, colored, wilfully murdered Luther White, colored, about four miles from here. Barker went to White's house, and, without any notice or cause whatever, knocked him once or twice in the head with a club, spattering his brains over the floor. The murderer, not satisfied, then took his knife and ripped White's abdomen open. Barker has been at large until yesterday, when he was brought into town by a crowd that had been on the lookout for him ever since he committed the deed, and delivered to the proper authorities. To-day the officer, with a guard, started with him to the county jail in Houston, which is about twenty miles from here. When about six miles from town they were met by an armed mob, who seized the prisoner, carried him a short distance into the woods and shot him dead. Barker pleaded earnestly for his life, but without effect. Justice was meted out to him properly by men of his own color.

robert-barker-okolona-1881-07-30.A4: Our readers will remember that we published some weeks since an account of the cruel and inhuman murder of Luther White by Rob. Barker. That one Peter Carlton also left his invalid wife in that neighborhood, with two little children, at the house of William Bowen. He is reported to be near Fort Dade, in Hernando county. Both left their wives penniless. The correspondent rightly thinks the heartless brutes should be looked after.

The Circuit Court for Duval county convenes on the first of November. Court will be held at the new court house on Bay street, between Laura and Hogan.

Fine Florida oranges are on the way to the Florida Exposition Department in Atlanta.

The Magnolia is the name of a new hotel soon to be erected at Green Cove Springs, on the St. John's, to be a magnificent piece of architecture, with one hundred and fifty rooms.

A party of young men recently dug into an Indian mound in Lake Hollingsworth, in Polk county, and exhumed therefrom human bones, old broken clay pottery and a large quantity of beads. One was a large silver bead, such as are worn by the chief of an Indian tribe.

A car load of cotton took fire between Midway and Quincy on Saturday, and several bales were injured before the fire could be extinguished.

The grand jury of Sumter county Circuit Court utterly failed to find out who were the parties that lynched J. J. Dickison, Jr., some two months ago.

The Ocala Lacon is issuing a daily during the session of the Circuit Court in that town.

A lodge of the Knights of Pythias was organized in Pensacola recently with thirty-eight charter members.

W. H. Ward, while at work on the City Hotel in Pensacola last week, fell from the second story and was badly crippled.

Our Banana correspondent writes, October 17th: "Cotton crop playing out. Orange trees shedding—dry, dry, dry. Corn and cotton short. Potatoes and cane short. Oranges only half size. Can't plant any greens patch. Things look blue."

Monticello Constitution: "The unfortunates who are under bonds to answer indictments by the United States Court are reminded that said court meets in Jacksonville on the first Monday in December, and it will be well for them to make arrangements so as to be present and respond at roll call."

Brooksville Crescent: "The carpeted earth of our ample forests is now bespangled with nameless millions of beautiful fall flowers. They are of every shade of color, from the deepest purple to the purest white. In some places there are acres covered with apparently a solid mass of snowy white blossoms. If at no other season, now at least, it must be admitted that Florida is a land of flowers."

The wheat crop in Roane county is said to be a failure, as a general thing.

A correspondent of the Roane County Democrat, who has visited the Oakdale Iron Works, in Roane county, has ascertained that 175 hands are employed regularly there. They manufacture, on an average, 60 tons of iron per day, and their daily expense is $500.

According to the Blount county Democrat, Montvale Springs will be run this season by Col. F. G. Martindale, and will be opened for guests Monday.

Blount county Democrat: Mr. Fred A. Fulton went over to Knoxville Tuesday last to take a position in Slocum's drug store. Fred is a nice young man, and is an experienced pharmacist. He has the good wishes of the entire community.

Greeneville has an ice-cream saloon.

George Canter has been sentenced to 3 years in the penitentiary by the circuit court at Greeneville for obtaining goods under false pretenses from G. B. Park & Co.

H. H. McNabb and James and G. W. Shockley have been appointed by Governor Hawkins census enumerators for Grainger county. Commissioner A. W. Hawkins has appointed A. B. Campbell land canvasser for Hancock county.

Nashville American: Governor Hawkins offers a reward of $250 for the apprehension and conviction of each of the unknown parties who, on the 11th inst., fired into the cabin of a colored man at Tracy City, without cause or provocation.

Early roasting ears begin to be abundant in market.

J. A. Abernathy has resigned the presidency of the Tennessee Valley Fair Association.

The body of a boy named John Sutton, 19 years old, was found last Monday in Chicamauga creek, near Chattanooga, where it was supposed the deceased had been bathing Sunday and was drowned. There were also suspicions of foul play, but they were not authenticated.

Thos. Hill, the man who has been in jail in Nashville, charged with having robbed A. G. Smith of government funds on Muscle Shoals last March, has been identified as Wm. Ryan, a member of the celebrated James Brothers' gang, the men who have been such a terror to the people of Missouri and some parts of Kentucky ever since the war. He has been taken to Missouri to answer a charge of having robbed the Concordia Bank of $35,000.

Mr. Beaman, with commendable enterprise, had all three of the street cars awaiting the closing of the exercises at the Opera-house last night, and they were well patronized and crowded by the returning citizens.

A negro man was jailed at Jonesboro last week for miscegenation, his wife being a full-blooded white woman.

The general manager of the famous Erlanger Railroad Syndicate, to whom the Alabama Great Southern Road belongs, was in Chattanooga this week, having just returned from a trip to Europe.

Concerts are to be given at Athens, the 23d; Sweetwater, 24th, and Loudon, 25th insts., by a splendid Knoxville organization, known as the Krutzsch Concert Company, consisting of Mr. Oscar Krutzch, Miss Cornelia Crozier, Miss Kate Deaderick, Mr. T. O. Deaderick, Mr. Frank Barker and Miss Clara Ware, accompanist.

John Kavanaugh was arraigned before Justice Allison yesterday, charged with a felonious assault on Elkanah Ballenger, of Grainger county, and was bound over to criminal court in the sum of $1,000, which bond was promptly given.

Dr. Key, the famous colored Keystone linament man, with his wonderful minstrel, "Black Sam," and another just like him, have been attracting crowds on the streets for the past two nights.

The Welsh Sunday-school picnic was enjoyed yesterday at Featherstone's grove, on the line of the Knoxville and Ohio railroad. There was a large attendance and it was a very pleasant occasion.

Thos. Shady, a deaf mute, was found on the train coming from Chattanooga yesterday by Prof. D. C. Hommel, out of money and attempting to make his way to New York, where he formerly lived. He is an intelligent and apparently worthy young fellow, who claims to have been a machinist in Memphis for about 2 years. Prof. Hommel kindly stood for his railroad fair to Knoxville, and gave him a note to the asylum, where here he will be properly cared for till he can get some assistance or work.
